That is true, finding a doctor to take cash or check for a base checkup is probably fine. But anything requiring extensive testing, x-ray, mri, or bone setting/cast would likely not be negotiable upfront, so you're left waiting for the bill and lucky if you can negotiate afterwards to get a reduced cost like insurers pay.

And in the case of emergency such negotiations go out the window. Somebody having a heart attack isn't going to negotiate and then decide, "I think I'll go look elsewhere." This is why I think healthcare is not such a great industry for the free market. When people's lives are stake, they'll pay literally anything to be treated. That complete disregard for price destroys competition and is the reason a 'less than severe' heart attack costs an average of $760,000 in the US, while a severe heart attack is something only a millionaire could actually afford to pay to get treated. Those costs have pretty absolutely nothing to do with the actual costs involved, but since the loss of life is involved people lose all notion of price sensitivity.

Our entire system of insurance is also pretty messed up. Insurers don't just "get a reduced cost." The prices are set 100% by the insurance company. The doctor sends them a number, but what they get back is 100% at the discretion of the insurance company. This again removes any notion of price competitiveness even for doctors. They're incentivized to just make sure they hit the top bracket of charges. This bastardization of insurance leads to the strange situation where you have to ensure that your hospital accepts your insurance instead of ensuring that your insurance accepts a hospital. And that's because what the hospital charges is completely irrelevant to the insurance.
